canonical_topic: Option value as a bounded percentage of the underlying price
definition: Black-Scholes-Merton's key insight is that an option's premium can be expressed as a fraction of the underlying's price, and that fraction is bounded by two extreme cases defined by the strike price.
core_idea: A call struck at zero must always end in the money regardless of the price distribution, so its premium must equal the underlying's price or an arbitrage exists; a call struck so high it can never be reached is worth nothing because it will never be exercised. Real options price somewhere between these two bounds.
key_points: A zero-strike call is always in the money no matter how future prices are distributed, so its premium must equal the underlying price to prevent arbitrage.
A call with an unreachably high strike will never be exercised, so its premium must be zero.
Most traded options have strikes between these extremes, so their premiums fall between 0% and 100% of the underlying's price.
relationships: Underlies the concept of delta / hedge ratio
trading_implications: An option's premium can be thought of as underlying price times a percentage (its hedge ratio) rather than derived independently each time.
